steps.message:
# Freeze store integrity maintenance

Ensure the `TextFileBasedViolationStore` maintains the integrity of its `stored.rules` index and files.

Setting `default.integrity` to `repair` will check the index and folder as they are on disk during initialization, even if the same folder was initialized before. Defaulting to `ignore` which checks nothing.

If an entry points to a path that is not a regular file directly within the folder, it is broken. This also applies if the file name is not a valid path.

If an entry is not broken and its file has no violations it is resolved. Files that only contain line breaks are also resolved.

Entries that point to the same file name are shared, even if nothing exists with that name. If multiple entries point to the same regular file they are also shared. Including through a symbolic or hard link. Even if that file is outside the folder.

The `TextFileBasedViolationStore` will not touch any shared entries or files that no entry points to. If an entry is shared and anything else it will remain shared.

When set to `repair` broken entries will be discarded without touching whatever they point to.

When set to `repair` resolved entries and the file they point to will be discarded. If a resolved entry is a symbolic link the file it points to will be deleted as well.

If using `repair` and saving no violations for a known rule it will forget the rule. Its entry will be removed and its file as well. Unless another entry is sharing that file. In which case only the entry will be removed. Even if it points outside the folder. If using `repair` and saving no violations for an unknown rule nothing will be saved.

If it cannot delete the file of a rule it is forgetting it will fail to save and leave the entry.

results.content:
==== Configuration

By default `FreezingArchRule` will use a simple `ViolationStore` based on plain text files.
This is sufficient to add these files to any version control system to continuously track the progress.
You can configure the location of the violation store within `archunit.properties` (compare <<Advanced Configuration>>):

[source,options="nowrap"]

Furthermore, it is possible to configure

[source,options="nowrap"]
.archunit.properties
----
# must be set to true to allow the creation of a new violation store

freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation=true

# can be set to false to forbid updates of the violations stored for frozen rules
# default is true
freeze.store.default.allowStoreUpdate=false
----

This can help in CI environments to prevent misconfiguration:
For example, a CI build should probably never create a new the violation store, but operate on
an existing one.

As mentioned in <<Overriding configuration>>, these properties can be passed as system properties as needed.
For example to allow the creation of the violation store in a specific environment, it is possible to pass the system property via

[source,options="nowrap"]
----

----

It is also possible to allow all violations to be "refrozen", i.e. the store will just be updated
with the current state, and the reported result will be success. Thus, it is effectively the same behavior
as if all rules would never have been frozen.

-Darchunit.freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation=true
----

Over time, the index file `stored.rules` and the individual violation files can get out of sync,
e.g. if violation files are deleted manually or if all violations of a rule have been fixed.
The violation store can maintain its integrity by itself:

[source,options="nowrap"]
.archunit.properties
----
# can be set to repair to maintain the integrity of the index and the violation files
# default is ignore, which checks nothing
freeze.store.default.integrity=repair
----

With `repair` the index and the violation files are checked as they are on disk every time the store is initialized.
Index entries that do not point to a regular file directly within the store folder are broken and will be discarded
without touching whatever they point to. Index entries whose file contains no violations (i.e. at most line breaks)
are resolved and will be discarded together with their file (and, if the file is a symbolic link, together with the file it points to).
Index entries that point to the same file name as another entry, or to the same regular file (also through symbolic or hard links),
are shared and will never be touched by the repair. Neither will any file that no index entry points to.
Furthermore, once there are no violations left for a frozen rule, the store will forget the rule,
i.e. remove its index entry together with its file (unless another entry shares that file, in which case only the entry is removed).
Rules without any violations will not be stored at all.
Note that the repair respects `allowStoreUpdate`, i.e. if updates are forbidden, the store will not be modified.

steps.message:
With `default.integrity=repair`, `TextFileBasedViolationStore` now repairs its `stored.rules` index and files as you described. The default, `ignore`, keeps the old behaviour. All 77 tests in the freeze package pass, including 18 new integrity tests and a new concurrency test, and ArchUnit's 14 architecture self-tests pass too. I couldn't run the Spotless format check because its formatter isn't cached for offline use, so formatting hasn't been verified.

**How it works:**
- **Re-checking on every initialize:** with `repair`, each `initialize` reloads `stored.rules` from disk, even if that folder was cached by an earlier initialization.
- **Broken, resolved, shared:** each entry is classified as you specified, and only entries that aren't shared get repaired. Two entries count as sharing a file if they have the same name, or the file system says they're the same file. That catches symbolic and hard links, including files outside the folder.
- **Saving with no violations:** the store deletes the file first and removes the entry only if that worked. If the delete fails it throws and leaves the entry. An unknown rule is never written.
- **Locking:** saving, reading and repairing now share one lock. Without it, a repair could see a file while another thread is rewriting it, think it's empty, and delete it.

**Choices I made where the spec didn't say:**
- **Bad setting value:** `default.integrity` is case-insensitive, and any value other than `ignore` or `repair` fails initialization with a clear message.
- **Updates disabled:** if `allowStoreUpdate=false`, the repair changes nothing and only logs a warning. That setting is documented as forbidding changes to any store file.
- **Delete fails during repair:** if a resolved file can't be deleted while initializing, the entry is kept and a warning is logged. Initialization doesn't fail; only `save` fails in that case, as you specified.
- **Forgetting a broken entry:** only the entry is removed. A file it points to outside the folder is never deleted, which matches how broken entries are handled during repair.
- **Lone `\r`:** a file containing only `\r` and/or `\n` characters counts as resolved, not just `\n` and `\r\n`.
- **Windows hard links:** where the file system gives no file IDs (Windows), every file in the store is compared against every other to find hard links. That gets slow if the store has many rules.

**A side effect you might not want:** with `repair`, a rule whose violations are all fixed is forgotten. If a violation of that rule comes back later, `FreezingArchRule` sees an unknown rule and freezes the new violation silently instead of reporting it. This follows directly from the spec, but it weakens regression protection.

The code changes are in `TextFileBasedViolationStore.java`, plus a new message-and-cause constructor in `StoreUpdateFailedException.java`. The new tests are in `TextFileBasedViolationStoreIntegrityTest.java`, with one added to the concurrency test. I documented the setting in the class Javadoc and in `docs/userguide/008_The_Library_API.adoc`. Nothing is committed.
